axes.model_access:
**Works with many models, and can connect local models.**

The official README lists 15+ providers:

**"15+ providers — Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Ollama, OpenRouter, Azure, Bedrock, and more"**

Three access modes:

- use an API key directly
- use a local model
- connect an existing Claude / ChatGPT / Gemini subscription via ACP

The local and self-hosted path is complete.

Ollama, Ollama Cloud, LM Studio all work.
Docker Model Runner and Ramalama also work.
Ramaalama goes through the Ollama provider.

Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint can also be connected.
`OPENAI_HOST` can point at a self-hosted vLLM / KServe.

Subscription access splits into two classes:

- CLI Provider: `cursor-agent`
- ACP Provider: `claude-acp` / `codex-acp`
  the latter passes goose's extensions to the other side as MCP

Two entry points for choosing a model.
One is the Desktop Models tab, the other is `goose configure`.

The official docs flag one thing: `goose configure` does not support entering custom model names.
In that case set `GOOSE_MODEL`, or use Desktop.

The official docs also state that tool calling currently performs best with Claude 4.
They also recommend consulting the BFCL leaderboard.
axes.runtime:
**Local-first, with all three forms.**

- desktop app: macOS / Linux / Windows
- full CLI: for terminal workflows
- embeddable API: GDK / SDK

Official README wording:

"A native desktop app for macOS, Linux, and Windows. A full CLI for terminal workflows. An API to embed it anywhere. **Built in Rust** for performance and portability."

Code runs on your machine.

Model requests either leave the network or hit a local model endpoint.

There is also `goose serve`.
Desktop starts it in the background by default; it is a local ACP server.

You can also run `goose serve` standalone on a remote VM and have Desktop connect to it.
axes.local_files:
**The built-in Developer extension reads/writes files and executes commands, with very broad default permissions.**

Tools listed on the Developer extension page:

- `shell` — executes commands, officially marked High risk
- `write` — creates / overwrites files, High
- `edit` — precise text replacement, High
- `tree` — lists directory trees, Low
- `read_image` — views images, Low

The official wording is blunt:

"goose can run system commands with your user privileges and edit any accessible file **without your approval**"

Two more points:

- MCP Roots shares the current working directory with roots-capable extensions
- extensions can run inside Docker containers (`--container` and the goose-in-docker tutorial)

There is also a separate Analyze extension for **semantic analysis and call graphs**.
axes.background:
**A local process; it cannot keep running after shutdown.**

CLI sessions end with the terminal.

Model requests originate on your machine.

**Non-interactive is not background**: `goose run` is just scripted execution.
It runs once and exits, still occupying a local process (see the tools axis).

**There are scheduled and remote entry points, but all depend on the local machine being online**:

- Recipes' scheduled runs (schedules)
- the `goose serve` ACP server
- pointing Desktop at a remote goose server
- Roaming Agents (connecting from another machine to a running goose)

When the host shuts down, tasks are interrupted.
axes.tools:
**MCP is a first-class citizen**: extensions are MCP servers.

Official README wording:

"Connect to **70+ extensions** via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) open standard"

**Two transports verified**:

- stdio: `--with-extension`, can carry ENV=val and an explicit name
- Streamable HTTP: `--with-streamable-http-extension <url>`

There is also `--with-builtin`.

**Built-in extensions** (official Browse Extensions page):

- Developer
- Computer Controller
- Memory
- Auto Visualiser (MCP-UI)
- Code Mode (calling MCP tools from JS)
- Summon (loads skills and dispatches sub-agents)
- Top of Mind
- Analyze, etc.

The **Extension Allowlist** can restrict which MCP servers are installable in an enterprise.
MCP Elicitation, MCP Roots and MCP Apps are also supported.

**Non-interactive command `goose run`** arguments:

- `-t "text"` / `-i file` / `-i -` (stdin)
- `--output-format json|stream-json`
- `--no-session`
- `-s` to switch to interactive
axes.context:
**Sessions land in a local SQLite database; resumable and forkable.**

The official CLI Commands page records one change:

since 1.10.0, sessions are stored in a SQLite database sessions.db, no longer a single .jsonl

Session operation commands:

- `goose session -r` — resume
- `--fork` — copy history into a new session
- `--edit` — edit the conversation in an editor
- `session list / rename / remove / export` — exportable as markdown / json / yaml

**Compaction**: the official changelog mentions this.

Compaction happens at tool boundaries of the unrolled agent loop.

**Memory**: the built-in Memory extension provides durable context,
i.e. cross-session information storage.

Top of Mind injects durable instructions each turn.
The official docs also have goosehints-style context-engineering techniques.
axes.permissions:
**The default is the most permissive tier, worth noting on its own.**

Official Developer extension page wording:

"goose runs in **Autonomous permission mode by default**"

That is: it executes shell commands and edits any accessible file without approval.

**Four permission modes** (`GOOSE_MODE` or `/mode` in-session):

- `auto` — no approval needed
- `approve` — every action requires review
- `smart_approve` — an AI decides which actions need review
- `chat` — all tools disabled

**Tool-level permissions** can also be set individually.

Under approve / smart_approve, each extension tool has three policies:

- Always allow
- Ask before
- Never allow

**Data surface**: the official Usage Data page states two things.

Collecting anonymous usage data requires **first-run consent**.
Consent can be changed at any time.

The diagnostics bundle `goose session diagnostics` includes session messages and configuration.
The official docs advise checking before sharing.

**Where model-inference data flows depends on the provider you choose**.
goose itself is an Apache-2.0 local program.
axes.fit:
Four kinds of people fit:

- those wanting a **local-first general agent whose provider can be swapped to anything (including local models)**, not just coding
- those needing both a desktop app and a CLI
- enterprises that need MCP-extension-centric capability with allowlist governance
- those wiring an agent into scripts or CI (`goose run --output-format json`)
